audience: People - skewing women - whose skin looks different in every mirror and every light, who cycle through products without knowing which one actually helps, whose routine grew complicated without getting better. They photograph their skin on bad days, compare themselves to filtered faces, and want private progress they can trust - not a public score, not another brand pushing product.

aesthetic: clean bathroom light, skincare minimalism, soft neutrals and warm whites, honest unfiltered skin close-ups, shelves with few chosen products
do: validate the confusion of not knowing what works; name the exact mirror-and-bathroom-light moment; keep claims cosmetic and visible-signal only; frame progress as a trend over weeks, not an overnight fix; let the app appear once as a quiet habit on a middle slide
dont: medical or dermatological claims, promising to cure acne or any condition, before/after miracle framing, shaming skin, brand-pushing or affiliate energy, public score comparisons, exclamation marks
context: Positioning from the App Store listing: skincare quickly becomes a chain of guesses - mirror, bathroom light, a drawer full of products that do not show what is actually changing. GlowKit is the calmer way to read the skin's visible signals, understand the next priority, and keep the routine alive without judgment, face-ranking, or brand pressure. Private by design: analysis quality is checked so progress photos compare fairly across light and angle. Sold as GlowKit Pro subscription. New app, no public ratings yet - content carries all the trust, so hooks should lean on symptom-of-confusion recognition (product cycling, light-dependent skin, routine overwhelm) rather than authority.
